newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin, under fire from foes, stays in hospital.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin, under fire from foes, stays in hospital.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, under fire from communists who say he should quit if he is unfit to rule, should face a decision soon from doctors who plan to operate on his heart.
Interfax news agency quoted top U.S. cardiologist Michael DeBakey as saying doctors would meet on Wednesday to decide when and whether to operate on the 65-year-old Russian president.
DeBakey, who conducted the world's first successful bypass surgery, will join the team of doctors advising the president, but is not expected to participate in the operation itself.

Yeltsin said earlier this month that he had agreed to have a heart operation. He has been in hospital for the last 10 days and doctors have expressed concern about whether he is fit enough to undergo surgery.
Top Russian surgeon Renat Akchurin suggested at the weekend that the operation might be delayed for six to eight weeks -- or even cancelled. Akchurin is expected to lead the operation.
He also said Yeltsin had probably had a heart attack during the presidential election campaign.
Russian communists, defeated by Yeltsin in the July election, accused the president and his team of misleading the electorate by concealing information.

"(Concealing the heart attack) amounts to falsification. The elections were not fair," Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov told Reuters at the Council of Europe's parliamentary assembly in Strasbourg.
Gennady Seleznyov, the communist speaker of the State Duma (lower house of parliament) said Yeltsin should resign if the surgeons refused to operate and told him to take life easy.
"The situation in Russia is such that (the president) cannot have an easy work schedule," Gennady Seleznyov told reporters.
The communists had a political boost on Tuesday when their candidate took first place in regional elections in the far eastern Amur region.
Early figures published by Interfax showed the communist candidate just ahead of the current administration chief. Final figures are likely on Wednesday.
The Kremlin had no fresh information on Yeltsin's health on Tuesday and could not confirm a news agency report that the president was due to meet Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
Yeltsin decreed last week that Chernomyrdin would stand in for him during surgery, as provided by the constitution, and has already transferred some of his powers to the prime minister.
Yeltsin disappeared from the public eye in late June, towards the end of a fierce campaign for reelection.

Aides initially said the president was tired and had lost his voice, but Yeltsin later admitted that he needed an operation. He said doctors had told him that the alternative was to lead a passive life.
The mounting doubts about the actual date of surgery -- and whether the operation will take place at all -- have unsettled Russia's embryonic financial markets.
Russian shares fell an average of three percent on Monday and prices tumbled further on Tuesday.
"It's really crashing, moving down with even some panic among brokers," said Alexei Genkin, sales desk manager at Alfa-Capital.
Yeltsin's illness coincides with a top-level meeting of international surgeons and cardiologists taking place in Moscow's exclusive President Hotel.
The doctors' get-together, a conference entitled blandly "The history of cardio-vascular surgery", has turned into a media circus where reporters and television crews almost outnumber doctors.
DeBakey and Russian cardiologist Leo Bokeria are due to hold a news conference at 5.30 p.m. (1330 GMT).
